conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days; it helps us spot anything from the normal “baby blues” to signs of depression or anxiety that deserve extra care. Everything you share stays between us unless safety is at stake, and there’s no “failing” grade—only information that guides the best support for you. I’ll read each question conversationally; just tell me what feels closest to your experience. Ready to begin?

1. Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I can still laugh—just not quite as easily as before. It’s not like I’ve lost my sense of humor, but little jokes or silly moments that would’ve cracked me up right away now feel kind of muted. Most days I manage a smile, but it takes a bit more effort.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I’ve been able to laugh, just not as much or as easily as I used to. Sometimes I’ll catch myself smiling, but it feels kind of quick and then it’s gone.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to some things—like when my mom brings dinner or when I can sneak in a shower without the baby crying—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. It’s more like “that’ll be nice” instead of really counting down the minutes like I did before she was born.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. When she wouldn’t settle in her crib, I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—like if I were a better mom she’d sleep. I know in my head that babies cry, but the thought still pops up that it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit. Sometimes I’ll suddenly worry that she’s too quiet or that her breathing sounds different, even when I can see she’s fine. It’s not all day—just quick flashes that I can usually talk myself down from, but they still catch me off-guard.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—nothing like my heart racing or anything. Just those quick little “what-if” scares about the baby, but they pass pretty fast.
Things have been getting on top of me
Some days, yeah. When she won’t nap and the dishes pile up, I feel like I’m running in circles. I usually get through it, but it feels heavier than it used to—like I’m always a step behind.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I do feel a little down sometimes, but it’s mostly just trouble drifting off because my mind keeps ticking through the next feed or whether I packed the diaper bag right. Once I’m asleep, I stay asleep—unless she wakes me.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—maybe a couple of days this week. It kind of comes and goes. I’m not walking around miserable all day, but there are moments when I just feel weepy and low, especially when I’m alone with the baby in the evening.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, I’ve cried… maybe twice since last week. Not all-day sobbing—just sudden tears when everything feels a bit too much, like when she wouldn’t latch and I felt useless. It lasts a few minutes, then I wipe my face and keep going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 11: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening – 2 wks post-delivery

Symptoms endorsed  
• Reduced ability to laugh/enjoy activities (anhedonia)  
• Intermittent sadness, “weepy” evenings, 2 crying spells in past week  
• Self-blaming cognitions (“I’m a bad mom”) when infant fusses  
• Transient, unprovoked worries about infant safety, quick to self-soothe  
• Overwhelm/coping strain on difficult days  

Associated factors  
• Mild sleep-onset difficulty (rumination re: infant care)  
• No current appetite/weight concerns queried  
• No self-harm ideation; no panic-level physiologic arousal  

Pattern  
Mild, fluctuating dysphoric mood with anxious cognitions, largely situation-dependent, absence of safety risk.

Screening significance  
Findings suggest subsyndromal depressive/anxious symptoms common in postpartum period; do not meet threshold for major depression yet impact daily coping. Continue monitoring, consider re-screen in 2–3 weeks (EPDS, PHQ-9) or sooner if worsening mood, functioning, or any safety concerns arise.
